title: Context is a budget
lead: Context engineering decides what task-relevant information the model has — and what it does not.
cues: Prompt engineering: how a task is described.
Context engineering: what information the model can access.
The window fills with every tool output.
Compaction frees space — at different thresholds and in different ways.
takeaway: Every token in the window competes for the model’s attention.
source: Mohsenimofidi et al. (2026), Context Engineering for AI Agents in OSS, MSR ’26, §1 · Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §7

title: Who actually writes context files?
lead: An empirical study scanned 10,000 popular GitHub projects for AI context files.
cues: Formats: Copilot instructions, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md.
Adoption is early: only 5% of mature projects.
AGENTS.md is the tool-agnostic convention, so it is studied in depth.
Most common pair: AGENTS.md with CLAUDE.md.
takeaway: Context engineering is real practice, but still early.
source: Mohsenimofidi et al. (2026), Context Engineering for AI Agents in OSS, MSR ’26, §3–4.1

title: What goes into AGENTS.md
lead: Projects describe conventions, contribution rules and architecture — rarely security.
cues: Top three: conventions, contribution guidelines, architecture.
Then: build and test commands — what an agent must run.
Rare: troubleshooting and security.
No shared structure yet across projects.
takeaway: Teams document how to work here, not how to stay safe.
source: Mohsenimofidi et al. (2026), Context Engineering for AI Agents in OSS, MSR ’26, §4.2, Table 1

title: Five ways to phrase an instruction
lead: The same convention can describe, order, forbid, explain or set a condition.
cues: Descriptive states facts; prescriptive gives orders.
Prohibitive sets boundaries — “never …”.
Explanatory adds the reason; conditional a situation.
Open question: which style changes agent behaviour most?
takeaway: How you phrase context is a design choice, not a detail.
source: Mohsenimofidi et al. (2026), Context Engineering for AI Agents in OSS, MSR ’26, §4.2

title: Context files are maintained artifacts
lead: Half the files never change; active ones are tuned instruction by instruction.
cues: 50% unchanged since they were added.
Active files: mostly add or reword instructions.
Few removals: files tend to grow.
Treat them like code: versioned, reviewed, tested.
takeaway: Context files co-evolve with the code they describe.
source: Mohsenimofidi et al. (2026), Context Engineering for AI Agents in OSS, MSR ’26, §4.3, Table 2

title: What stays in context, what waits on disk
lead: Harnesses keep the always-loaded context small and move the rest behind a tool call.
cues: Always loaded: instructions, schemas, a skill catalog, small memory files.
On demand: a skill’s full text only when it is used.
On disk: full history, searchable but out of the window.
Hermes caps memory at a few thousand characters on purpose.
takeaway: Load context just in time, not just in case.
source: Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §7, §15 · Nous Research, Hermes Agent docs; Alejandro AO (2026), Hermes architecture

title: Subagents are context engineering
lead: A subagent spends tokens exploring in its own context and returns one short report.
cues: The orchestrator delegates several prompts at once.
Workers start with a fresh context and keep their search noise.
The parent keeps only the call and the reports.
Hermes runs one child by default; in Pi Durable a subagent is a conversation owned by a tool call.
takeaway: The harness decides what the orchestrator never sees.
source: Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §11, Rec. 12 · Earendil (2026), Pi Durable, earendil.com/posts/pi-durable
